title: The Hidden Work of Growth #1: Just be more confident
author: Elina
summary: Executive coach Elina opens a four-part series on capability development by dismantling the vague, common leadership feedback "you just need to be more confident." Through a composite client case study (Svetlana, recently promoted and still uncomfortable occupying her new role's authority), the piece breaks confidence down from an abstract personality trait into a collection of concrete, addressable moments: self-conscious thoughts, bodily tightness, vocal pitch, and hedging language. Her key reframe is that a habit like hedging often isn't simply a flaw to eliminate but a strategy serving a real purpose, such as avoiding conflict or the appearance of arrogance, so coaching aims to give the client more conscious choice rather than demanding she become a different person. The piece closes by insisting that real behavioral change requires insight, experimentation, practice, and accountability, not advice alone, positioning "just be more confident" as exactly the kind of unhelpfully simple directive the series exists to unpack.
points: Reframes 'just be more confident' from a vague personality trait into a set of concrete, addressable components: self-conscious thoughts, bodily tightness, vocal pitch, and hedging language.
Uses a composite client case (Svetlana, newly promoted and still uncomfortable with authority) to demonstrate how abstract feedback fails to translate into actionable behavior change.

Argues that a habit like hedging often serves a real protective purpose (avoiding conflict, avoiding the appearance of arrogance) rather than being simply a flaw, which changes how a coach should approach eliminating it.
Insists genuine behavior change requires insight, experimentation, practice, and accountability rather than advice alone, positioning generic confidence tips as fundamentally insufficient.
quotes: My experience tells me that when you hear the word just, be ready for something that is way more complicated than it sounds. Confidence is one of those complex things that you can't simply switch on, like adjusting the volume on a speaker.

A self-conscious thought that pulls your attention away from the conversation. The tightness you feel in your body when you are about to speak. The pitch or speed of your voice. Hedging and filler words.
When we want just confidence, it can feel like a personality trait you either have or do not have. But once you start looking at the actual pattern, you have something to work with.

Perhaps Svetlana's hedging was not simply a bad habit. Perhaps it was serving a purpose. It might have been her way of remaining open, avoiding unnecessary conflict or protecting herself from being seen as arrogant.
Changing the pattern of your thinking and behaviour takes more than advice. It takes insight, experimentation, practice and accountability.
